$comment: TEMPLATE — safe defaults for any machine. Run `npm run setup` (or scripts/install.ps1) to generate a config.json tailored to your displays, or copy this file to config.json and edit by hand. config.json is gitignored, so your local settings stay yours. Anything you omit falls back to these values.

display.$comment: Which monitor the HUD takes over. strategy: 'smallest' picks the lowest-resolution display, which is almost always the little sensor panel — it needs no configuration and is the default for that reason. 'bounds' pins a specific monitor by the position of its top-left corner (run `npm run displays` to get yours); prefer it if you have two displays of the same size. 'index' uses the Nth display as Electron enumerates them — avoid it, the order is not stable across reboots and hot-plugs. 'primary' and 'largest' also exist. If the chosen strategy matches nothing, 'fallback' is used.

window.$comment: clickThrough makes the HUD ignore the mouse entirely — clicks pass through to whatever is underneath, so you can never accidentally focus or drag it. Turn it off if you want to interact with the panel. Use the tray icon to quit or toggle this at runtime.

polling.$comment: fastMs drives load, temperature, clocks and network. slowMs drives things that barely change (disk capacity, uptime). 1000 is a good default; 500 is smoother and costs more CPU.

nvidiaSmi.$comment: NVIDIA GPU telemetry. Needs no elevation and no extra install — nvidia-smi ships with the driver. On AMD or Intel graphics leave this enabled but expect the GPU panel to read '--'; LibreHardwareMonitor below covers those GPUs for temperature and load.

libreHardwareMonitor.$comment: OPTIONAL but strongly recommended. The only way to get CPU package temperature, CPU power draw and fan RPM: Windows exposes no public API for them. Install it, then enable Options > Remote Web Server > Run (scripts/install.ps1 configures this for you) and run it as Administrator. The HUD works fine without it — those fields just read '--'.
libreHardwareMonitor.$fanSensor: Which fan header to show. null auto-picks the first fan reporting a non-zero speed, which is a guess — many motherboards label headers generically as 'Fan #1'..'Fan #7' with no indication which one is the CPU cooler. Run `npm run doctor` to list yours, then pin it by exact name, e.g. "Fan #2".

network.$comment: Read via Get-NetAdapterStatistics rather than systeminformation, which silently reports zero for any adapter whose name contains a space (e.g. 'Wi-Fi 6'). Leave interface null to auto-pick the busiest adapter reporting Up; set an exact adapter name from `Get-NetAdapter` to pin one.

nowPlaying.$comment: Reads the Windows global media session, so it shows whatever is playing — Spotify, a browser tab, VLC — with no API key or login. Needs no setup.

weather.$comment: Open-Meteo — no API key, no signup, no account. Set your coordinates to switch it on; while they are null the weather block simply does not render. Deliberately does NOT geolocate by IP: that would send your address to a third party at every start, and would land on your ISP's city or your VPN exit anyway. Two decimal places (about 1 km) is plenty — the forecast grid is 1-11 km, so more precision only leaks your location. units: metric or imperial.

ping.$comment: Internet reachability. Times a TCP handshake rather than shelling out to ping.exe: no process spawn per sample, and ICMP is filtered on many networks so a failed ICMP ping is a poor proxy for 'no internet'. Reports the median of the last few samples.

sensors.$processes: Feeds the ORDERS panel: which processes are actually using the CPU and the RAM, grouped by name. Read through a PowerShell helper rather than systeminformation, whose processes() call costs about 900ms of CPU every time and does not cache - an absurd price for a panel whose job is to watch CPU, not consume it. The helper holds the previous sample and derives real CPU percentages itself; see scripts/processes-loop.ps1.

$theme: espresso (warm brushed steel, cream manometer dials), neon (cyan/magenta cyberpunk), blueprint (cyanotype board, white paper dials), daylight (paper and ink - the light theme, for a panel by a window), slate (flat graphite, no texture, stays out of the way), or phosphor (P1 oscilloscope tube: blue-green bloom, scanlines, monospace). Any of them can be recoloured token by token via ui.themeOverrides below, or from the settings page. Every status ramp is validated for colour-vision separation and contrast against its own surface - run `npm run themes` to re-check them.

ui.$comment: Everything below is editable live from the settings page (tray icon > Settings...), which previews each change on the panel before you commit it. Editing here by hand works exactly the same; the file is the source of truth either way.
ui.$panels: Hides whole sections. A hidden panel is never placed on a page at all, so the remaining ones get its room rather than leaving a gap.
ui.$history: How much past the LOG BOOK panel keeps. Costs nothing to collect: these are the readings the panel already takes every second and used to throw away. Kept in the main process, so peaks survive a HUD reload - a peak that silently resets on reload is worse than no peak, because it still looks authoritative.
ui.$typography: This panel is read from across a desk, so how big 'big' should be depends on the desk. scale drives type, dial diameter and row heights together, so raising it keeps the layout in proportion instead of letting type outgrow its plate. Past about 1.2 the all-in-one layout runs out of height, which is the point at which rotation starts to pay for itself. family/numerals take a preset id ('bahnschrift', 'consolas', 'segoe', ... - the settings page lists them all) or a raw CSS font stack; null means the theme's own choice. Local faces only: the HUD may boot with no network, so a webfont would be a blank panel waiting on a download.
ui.$themeOverrides: Layered on top of whichever base theme is selected, so switching themes keeps your edits. Keys are the theme's custom properties without the leading dashes: brass, surface, ink, mark-crit, dial-face and so on. Halos are derived from the readout colours rather than set here. Anything not listed falls back to the theme.
ui.$rotation: Cycling pages trades instant recognition for legibility. Spatial constancy is most of what makes an ambient panel readable - you learn where a number lives and stop having to look properly - and rotation gives that up: some of the time the reading you want is simply not on screen. It earns its place on a panel too small to hold everything legibly, and the cost is paid down three ways: the bar never rotates, alertOverride pulls the gauges page forward and holds it while a reading is out of range, and a page with a 'when' condition is skipped rather than shown empty. transition 'fade' is the default because direction is what makes motion hard to ignore out of the corner of your eye. Off here keeps the classic single-screen layout, pixel for pixel.

rotation.$pages: Each page should answer a DIFFERENT question. Rotation is only worth its cost if waiting for the next page gets you something you could not already see; a set of pages showing the same panels at different sizes is a wait in exchange for nothing. The five panels below the classic six exist only because rotation made room for them: processes (what is using the CPU and RAM), storage (disk read/write rates, endurance, free space), trends (temperature and load over time, with peaks and time-above-threshold), forecast (next 12 hours and 5 days), pressure (every fan header, board temp, VCore, GPU power headroom).

thresholds.$comment: Where the dial's printed danger zone begins, and where the ready lamp changes state. Celsius for temperatures, percent for the rest.
thresholds.$driveTemp: NVMe drives idle warm and start throttling around 70C, so these are deliberately lower than the CPU numbers.

power.$comment: Holds off the display-sleep timer so the HUD monitor stays lit and Windows never reshuffles your windows off it.

admin.$comment: The settings page, reachable from the tray icon. It writes config.json and nothing else - it runs no commands and reads no file outside its own directory. Bound to loopback, where only this machine can reach it. Binding it to a LAN address requires a token to be set first and is refused without one; the service also checks the Host and Origin headers, so a web page you have open cannot reach it or rewrite your config. Set enabled to false to not listen at all.
